content.thinking:
I'm sketching out the design plan for a red panda rendered at realistic proportions, balancing on a mossy stone with one paw raised and tail curved for balance, styled in a Genshin-esque cel-shaded anime look.

Thinking through accent details: glowing teal-green dendro runes on the stone, scattered fireflies, and a small gold-trimmed ribbon or charm on the panda's collar to stay tasteful while respecting anatomical accuracy. For the model structure, the stone sits on the floor as part of the overall piece with a single root joint anchored at the panda's hips, giving a total height around 0.55 meters including ears.

For the pose, I'm settling on a quadruped stance with all four paws on the stone, legs straight but slightly separated for stability, tail curved upward in an S-shape for balance, and the head lifted with a slight tilt. I'm now working out exact measurements — stone top at 0.20 m, paw placement, and shoulder height around 0.24 m — to keep the proportions believable.

Now I'm sketching the body dimensions: a stocky, rounded torso about 0.45 m long and 0.09 m wide, a broad head with pointed snout and large triangular ears, and a bushy ringed tail roughly 0.45 m long with alternating dark red and cream bands. For the stone, I'm picturing a lumpy boulder built from scaled icosahedron shapes with flat shading, painted mottled grey, topped with moss cards and hanging fern leaves for texture.

For glowing accents, I'm planning small glowing octahedra as dendro motes and a glowing rune circle rendered as a decal texture on the stone's face. Then I'm defining the red panda's color palette -- rusty orange back, dark brown-black belly and legs, white facial markings with dark tear-lines, black nose, and alternating rust-toned tail rings -- before laying out the skeleton starting with the hip root and a spine chain following a curved path from hips to chest.

Now I'm working out the short neck chain, sketching a path of just a few points between the chest and head base and figuring out how many joints and spans that requires, before positioning the head joint to aim forward from the neck's end.

Then I'm planning the tail as a raised S-curve path with several catmull points rising up and back, setting a six-joint chain for it, and sketching the front legs' positions — shoulder joints and paw targets calibrated to short red panda proportions so the feet land correctly on the stone surface.

Working out the paw geometry as rounded dark brown shapes with toes, then placing the front leg's shoulder and target coordinates to compute segment distances for the limb chain.

For the hind leg, I'm figuring out hip and target positions with knee-forward, hock-back bends to approximate a semi-plantigrade red panda foot, planning separate paw boxes resting on the stone surface.

Similarly for the front limb, path goes shoulder-elbow-wrist-toe, with the wrist angled forward toward the toe tip. For toes, I'll keep it simple with small sphere or cone-shaped claw bumps and dark pads rather than full digit joint chains, since adding individual joints per toe would eat into the joint budget too fast.

Now shifting to the head: positioning the skull sphere broadly with cheek tufts, a short rounded snout with a black nose tip, and a small separate lower jaw capsule that can rotate on its own joint. For the ears, I'm thinking big rounded triangular shapes with pale fringe on the inside and darker coloring on the outer back, matching the red panda's distinctive ear pattern.

For the eyes, I'm leaning toward a Genshin-style anime look with large shiny decal eyes, considering an emerald-teal iris color to complement the orange fur and tie into a dendro-inspired glow theme, sized appropriately against the roughly 0.17-wide face.

White patches get painted directly onto the skull so they won't conflict with the cheek ruffs, which I'll handle separately as spiky extrudes below eye level. For head coloring, I'm defining a function based on position within the head region — rust base tone, white muzzle and cheeks, and dark tear markings.

Working out the facial paint logic using local coordinates relative to the head center: white covers the lower muzzle, cheeks, and chin in a zigzag pattern, while the forehead stays a rust-tan color, the nose is black, and a white "spectacle" patch sits above each eye, with dark tear stripes running from eye to mouth corner.

Now I'm sizing and placing the eye decals relative to the skull's scaled dimensions, positioning them symmetrically at an angle from the head's center, then shaping the snout as a smaller scaled sphere offset downward and forward, topped with a tiny black nose sphere and a highlight for shine, plus a swept line for the mouth.

I'm thinking through accessories too -- adding a collar band around the neck in deep teal with gold trim, a hanging gold leaf pendant with a glowing green gem, and decorative tassel cards for a Genshin-style ornament. For the moss stone base, I'm planning to use a low-poly icosahedron scaled into a flattened boulder shape with faceted shading and a cel-shaded grey-blue stone material, then add mottled texture on top.

Now I'm figuring out where moss patches appear using a noise-based threshold on the surface normal's vertical component, painted in bright lime-green with light/dark variation, while also working out the ellipsoid math so the stone's curved top stays level enough for the panda's paws to rest convincingly at their offset positions.

I'll stack a bigger lower slab beneath it, scatter smaller rocks and a pebble around the base, and add a moss cap by painting the flat top surface where normal.y is high.

Now I'm working out the stone layering: a wide base rock, then a narrower mid-level rock sitting on top, each with its own thickness and vertical offset so the top surface lands at y=0.20, and sizing their outlines to fit the panda's footprint.

I want to scatter smaller pebbles and a step rock near the front for visual variety, then add moss details — green tuft cards on the top edges and sides where the surface normal faces upward, plus hanging moss at the rims, and small Genshin-style flowers for color accents.

Now I'm thinking about mushrooms, glowing dendro motes, and a sigil ring decal on the stone's front face, along with an SVG filigree plate combining a gold swirling border with a glowing green leaf glyph for that ancient-ruin, gold-inlaid feel.

For the surface, since smoothing makes walls curved rather than flat, I realize using a decal projection (b.decal with position and direction) is the right approach for curved stone faces. I'll split it into two decals — a non-glowing gold filigree border and a separate glowing glyph layered inside it — then place the rune decal on the stone's front wall facing +Z, which is the visible side across the camera angles.

Now I'm thinking through the panda's fur details: using flat cel-shaded fur cards with zigzag edges for cheek ruffs, chest fluff, tail-ring edges, and ear fringes, drawing them as white locks that get tinted via the card color property rather than baking color into each texture.

For the coat palette, I'm settling on a rust-red base for the back, slightly darker maroon on the flanks, dark chestnut-black underside, and black-brown legs, with a lighter orange-yellow highlight strip running along the spine to suggest countershading.

Composing the body paint logic now...

For the red panda's legs, I'm thinking black-brown from the elbow down, matching the belly tone, with darker paws at the tips.

Still writing paint functions for the tail rings...

Confirming nested paints read the current state correctly. For the tail I'm thinking bushy and thick near the base tapering to a rounded tip, with a radius array shaping that curve and a sweep of ten sides to get the rust-colored fluffy locks along the edges as it sweeps backward and up.

For the balancing pose, I'm plotting a path where the tail extends behind the rump and curves upward, with the tip curling slightly forward -- keeping total height moderate so it doesn't overwhelm the head proportions. For the body, I'm planning a sweep along the spine with varying radii to get thicker rounded hips tapering toward the chest, using an elliptical cross-section through a catmull-rom path along the spine joints.

The sweep along the chain gives the centerline from hips to tip with rounded caps at each end, so with a body length around 0.34 plus caps, total is roughly 0.52. I'm adjusting the path to extend further, from -0.17 to 0.19, and tuning the chest radius for the ellipse profile.

Going for a chibi-style proportion where the head is slightly larger relative to the body, since red pandas have fairly wide heads compared to their bodies, and keeping the eyes big for that cute look. Now I'm listing out the parts needed: for the stone, I need the base slab, pebbles, rock chunks, moss, flowers, mushrooms, and glow decals; for the panda, the body coat sweep, chest bib, neck, head, ears, eyes, nose, and whiskers.

I'm adding more fur details like cheek ruffs, legs, paws, toes, claws, tail with painted rings, a collar with pendant and tassel, and maybe a small glowing leaf sprig on the head as a playful touch instead of a literal hat.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy—hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, ear hinges, tail segments, and leg joints—totaling around 35, and thinking through the side convention where s=1 represents the model's right in local space.

I'm settling on using world coordinates consistently rather than local space to avoid confusion, defining the head joint position and skull center numerically, and sketching out the skull geometry using a scaled sphere while considering a low-poly, faceted cel-shaded look rather than a perfectly smooth sphere.

For the cheek ruffs, I'm thinking through how red pandas have distinctive tufted cheek fur pointing outward and back -- I'll approximate this with small spike or cone shapes placed on the cheek surface in groups of three per side, angled outward and backward in a cream color.

For ears, I'm working out how to extrude a rounded triangle outline positioned near the top of the head, tilted outward, figuring out the coordinate system for the width and height directions of the ear plane.

Setting up symmetric ear geometry...

Defining the ear outline shape...

I'll skip the ear tufts and instead add a tear-line mark characteristic of red pandas—a dark chestnut streak painted from below the eye down toward the mouth, defined using normalized local coordinates relative to the head center and a curved center-line function.

I'm also adding white cheek patches lower on the face, a zigzag boundary, muzzle white, and small white eyebrow spots above each eye mimicking red panda "spectacles," since the eye decal itself keeps its dark almond shape and I want the surrounding fur painted darker there to match the real animal's eye patches rather than rust or white.

Working out placement now: eyes scaled small and positioned with slight outward angle on the skull front, the muzzle sized and offset below center with its tip protruding forward, and a small black nose placed at the very tip. I'm also planning ink lines for a philtrum and smile curve sweeping down the muzzle surface.

Then I'm sketching the lower jaw as a rounded capsule joint hinged near the base of the head, keeping the mouth closed and skipping extra details like fangs or tongue. Now I'm starting on the whisker placement, planning three per side.

Beyond that I'm figuring out the fur cards — flat curved tuft shapes that get tinted by color, used to add fluffiness at the chest ruff, cheeks, ear fringe, and leg fur, plus denser tufts along the tail edge for that Genshin-style cel-shaded look.

I'm also designing the paws with scaled dark spheres, small toe spheres with ink outlines, and tiny cream claw cones, positioned so they sit embedded slightly in the stone surface. For the legs, I'm setting up a joint chain starting with shoulder and wrist coordinates for the front limbs.

I'm computing the elbow bend by solving for the perpendicular offset needed to satisfy the limb segment lengths, checking whether the resulting elbow position would land inside or outside the body's radius so the pose stays physically plausible.

I'm making the leg lengths closer to straight to avoid an unnatural V-shaped bend, and adjusting upper limb thickness for front legs versus the thicker hind thighs. Now I'm setting target joint positions for the hind leg -- hip, knee, ankle, and toe -- aiming for a plantigrade foot stance.

I'm computing the knee position so it bends forward and emerges naturally below the belly, and adding a rounded haunch sphere to help mask the hidden thigh mass within the body silhouette.

Now I'm figuring out how to assign bones along the leg chain for smooth skinning, including separate toe spheres on the tip bones for the paws, then turning to the collar — sweeping a neck path from chest to head with a joint chain positioned to sit just below the wide head so it stays visible.

For the collar itself, I'm cutting a loop at the base of the neck through the neck sweep rather than the body sweep so it doesn't intersect other geometry, then sweeping that loop into a thin ribbon. I'm weighing color options against the fur and considering a rich forest green with gold accents instead of a teal.

For the pendant, I'm placing a gold ring with a glowing green gem at the chest, found via a ray cast against the body surface, with a thin gold chain draped down from the collar. I'm also considering gold tassels and two ribbon tails trailing from a collar knot at the back.

I want gold filigree dots spaced along the collar, plus a small leaf tilted between the ears and tiny glowing motes floating near the gem and tail tip for an elemental touch. For stone decals, I'm targeting the main slab geometry with a positioned texture decal near its surface.

Working out the main slab's extrusion axes: with x and y basis vectors as chosen, the thickness runs along -Y, so centering it at y=0.12 with 0.16 thickness puts the top face at y=0.20, keeping everything symmetric about the slab's center.

Now I'm defining the irregular outline of the slab in the x-z plane, a roughly rounded shape spanning about 0.3 units in each direction with ten points to give it a natural, non-circular silhouette. I'm treating the panda's body as centered slightly behind z=0, so I need to make sure its paws align properly with this outline.

Then I'm making the stone narrower than the slab to give the panda a sense of precarious balance -- stone width around 0.34 against a body width of 0.2, with a broader flat slab base beneath it. I'm thinking through paint details: mossy coloring on the upper surface and cracks on the stone using patch-based line techniques.

Writing moss/stone paint logic...

I want this stonePaint applied consistently across all stone parts—base slab, main slab, pebbles. Then I'm adding glow motes, small lime-green dendro octahedrons near the stone and tail, plus eight fireflies, and planning lathe-cap mushrooms with red-orange tops and white dots.

I'm settling on warm-pink caps with cream dots and pale cream stems, clustering three mushrooms at the base front-right, then adding card-based flowers with five white-lilac petals and yellow centers near the moss top, along with fern frond and moss tuft cards at the base.

For the moss tufts I'm drawing multiple grayish-white blades tinted by a moss paint color, keeping shading stable by using a fixed lime tone and texture pair. I'm scattering moss cards across the top of the slab where the surface normal faces upward enough, sharing a single mask function between the paint evaluation and the card placement filter so coverage stays consistent before moving on to vines.

Rather than a draped vine, I'm doing a hanging moss fringe along the rim: finding hits near the edges of the main slab with moderate upward normals, then flipping the card frames 180 degrees so they dangle down and cover the rim wall. I'm tallying up the texture atlas needs across fur, moss clumps, hanging strands, flowers, ferns, eyes, runes, filigree, and tassels, then checking the sample directory and kit imports before writing the actual file, keeping an eye out for unused variable issues.

Setting up the color palette and material definitions...

Layering fur edge effects...

Writing fur edge logic for legs...

For the tail, I'm computing a striping pattern using segment position along the tail combined with a zigzag offset based on cross-section, alternating between two colors per segment — with the tip forced dark and the base near the body staying rust-colored.

Now I'm moving on to the head paint, building it relative to a defined skull center point.

Still defining facial zones...

Muzzle and chin regions stay white, blending with the skull coloring. Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, building the spine chain from hips upward with a smooth curve path.

Continuing the chain setup, I'm adding the neck segments attached to the spine's tip joint, making sure the start position matches the chest to keep everything connected properly.

Now I'm placing the head joint at the end of the neck chain, then working out the jaw joint position relative to the head using local offsets for forward and downward distances, adjusting the values so the hinge sits near the rear of the cheek.

I'm reasoning through the skull and snout sphere dimensions to figure out where the lower jaw capsule should sit so it tucks naturally under the snout without clipping the skull's bottom edge.

Now I'm placing the muzzle box and nose sphere coordinates, then moving on to position the eye decals around the skull's surface using azimuth and elevation angles, and finally setting up the ear base anchor points near the skull's top.

I'm checking whether these ear axis vectors need to be orthonormal, but comparing to how the doc itself used non-orthogonal directions elsewhere suggests it's fine as-is. Computing the cross product of the ear's x and y directions tells me the normal points forward, with the sign flipping depending on which side (s=1 or s=-1) the ear is on.

Now I'm working out the paint logic for the ear surface, computing a width function along the ear outline and deciding where to shade the inner fur white versus the outer fur rust-colored based on local coordinates and whether the face normal points into the ear or outward.

I'm sketching the ear's outline points for a rounded, pointed triangular shape typical of a red panda, setting thickness and bevel values. Then I'm thinking through how to build the legs as sweeps along joint chains, defining the path through shoulder, elbow, wrist, and tip points.

Positioning the front limb joints, I work out where the wrist and paw should sit, calculating a flattened sphere for the paw and planning small toe spheres on the front foot.

Setting bend hints for front and hind limbs, and defining the hind leg joint chain from hip to toe with the foot positioned to sweep flat against the stone surface.

Now I'm working out knee offset geometry using the triangle formed by the two 0.085 segment lengths and the hip-to-ankle distance, computing the half-chord and perpendicular height to place the knee joint correctly.

For the hind toes, I'm placing small spheres just forward of the foot's tip joint. Then I'm positioning the tail root inside the rump's rounded rear cap—since the body sweep ends around z=-0.26 with the cap, the tail's first joint sits at z=-0.21/-0.22, parented to the hips, with the path curving upward and backward from there.

Now I'm defining the tail path with increasing count for smoothness and a tapered bushy radius profile, but checking the overall height—0.79 feels too tall, so I'm considering shortening the curve's endpoint and re-measuring the tail's total length against a realistic 0.37-0.47m target.

I'm trimming the path segments down to about 0.44m total length, reshaping the tail's curve points, and verifying the tail radius stays thick near the base while thinning toward the tip. With the tail bottom clearing the stone and the tip height balancing against the ear height, the overall max height comes out to roughly 0.66m, which looks right.

Now I'm sketching the body sweep: a tapered ellipse cross-section running along the spine chain from hips to chest, with radius functions shrinking slightly toward the tip. Writing sweep radius function...

Checking vertical placement: body centered around y≈0.385-0.40 with belly near 0.30 and top near 0.485, legs visible below, stone top clearing at 0.20. Also placing haunch spheres scaled for hip bulges, attached to the hind leg's hip joint for natural articulation.

Adding small shoulder blobs where needed, cream cheek ruff spikes on the head, and a tiny leaf-shaped hat ornament between the ears, built as an extruded outline with a sharp tip and slight tilt, sized and oriented to sit naturally on top of the head.

Now I'm thinking about the collar: I want a thin loop around the neck using a surface cut from the neck sweep. I need to figure out exactly where to place this loop, since the neck bone spans from the chest cap up toward the head, and I want it positioned at a reasonable midpoint without clipping into the chest or head geometry.

I'm testing a neck centerline from (0,0.408,0.18) to (0,0.445,0.285) with radius 0.07, placing the collar around t≈0.5 where z≈0.235, and comparing against the chest's larger radius at z=0.18 to see where the two surfaces actually meet.

The chest cap narrows significantly by z=0.235, giving a radius of about 0.058, which is smaller than the neck's 0.07 -- so the neck pokes outside the chest in that region. Checking the head's vertical extent (y 0.381-0.529) against the neck's range (y 0.36-0.5), it looks like the neck stays visible beneath and behind the head for z<0.257, roughly a 5cm band where a collar ribbon of radius 0.075 and width 0.025 would fit.

I'm placing the collar as a ring of points around the neck axis at a specific point along its length, then sweeping a tube along a closed Catmull-Rom curve through those ring points to form the band -- slightly larger radius than the neck so it sits just outside it. I'm considering whether to make it a flat ribbon instead of a round tube, but the orientation math for a flat cross-section gets complicated, so I'll stick with a round tube plus thin decorative rings on either side.

For the pendant, I'm figuring out where it should hang on the chest -- casting a ray forward from roughly chest height into the body's surface to find the exact front contact point, then offsetting it slightly outward so the pendant sits just above the skin rather than embedded in it.

I'm planning to add a gold ring with a glowing green diamond (an octahedron) set inside as the pendant's centerpiece, and considering whether to add a tassel of hanging cards below it, though I'm deciding to keep scope reasonable and skip the bow/ribbon details at the collar to avoid over-complicating the model.

I'm also sketching a fur tuft SVG texture as a curved flame-like shape in white, meant to be tinted later.

For moss I'm drawing explicit colored blade shapes with gradient greens like lime and darker tones, since those won't need tinting since colors are baked in directly.

For hanging moss I need strands pointing downward with the root edge oriented at top since the drawing will appear flipped when viewed from downstream. For the flower, I'm planning a stem with five radial petals as rotated ellipses around a center point, with the card standing upright along the surface normal so the flower faces along the flow direction, rooted at the bottom.

Now I'm sketching a simple fern frond with a central stalk and leaflets, then moving to decal designs: a glowing green rune/leaf glyph decal, and a separate gold-bordered filigree plaque with transparent interior so the stone shows through, layering the glowing glyph decal on top at a slightly different lift to avoid z-fighting flicker.

For the tassel I'm thinking through hanging orientation—drawing the knot and ball at the bottom with strands fanning upward so it reads correctly when hung upside down. I'm also setting up the eye texture with iris and blush colors, and placing small glowing octahedron motes attached to the hips bone, reasoning that floating or stone parts without a natural joint should default to the hips bone.

For the stone's rigging, I'm working out whether it should attach to a root joint separate from hips so it doesn't inherit hip rotation, settling on creating a "base" root joint with hips as its child, and considering whether to treat hips itself as the first spine joint to avoid duplicating a spine1 joint at the same location.

I'm starting to draft the full implementation now, importing the builder, frame, IK limb helper, math/rng, paint and texture utilities, and toon-kit pieces like the eye, fur edge, and ink styling.

Now I'm defining the moss mask function using surface normal and noise to blend lichen patches onto stone, with a lit moss color, a darker edge ink tone, and a base stone paint, combining them based on mask thresholds.

Adding crack detection logic...

Now I'm laying out the stone parts — base slab, main slab, scattered pebbles using scaled icosahedron shapes with flat shading and stone paint — plus a front step rock and back rock. Then I'm setting up fur card scattering along the tail sweep surface.

Still defining fur card scatter logic...

Painting the coat color at each card's root position and normal, placing cheek fur against the skull surface, and skipping the chest bib detail. Eyes and glints are already handled in texture, so I'm adding a tiny white highlight sphere for nose shine plus nostril line details on the muzzle. For glow effects I'm applying flat colors to parts and scaling an octahedron for the gem, then checking whether decal() returns a Part so I can wrap it in glow() for rune decorations.

I'm confirming decal targets work on the main slab part, then adding small toadstools and flower-themed cards, and working out dimensions for the gold ring. Now I'm defining the stone outline shape as a set of (x,z) coordinate points to extrude into a slab with thickness, bevel, and smoothing, making sure the lowest points stay within a small floor allowance so the base doesn't sink too far below ground level.

Now I'm working out the mid-slab outline coordinates similarly, choosing a thickness and bevel radius that stays under half the thickness, and checking that the overhang this creates near the rim looks intentional rather than broken. I'm also checking that paw placement stays within the stone's width and that the head and body extents overlap correctly so the head overhangs the body for a natural look, then considering how the bevel rounds the rim inward and shrinks the flat top area where the paws need to sit.

Then I'm scattering small pebble rocks around the base slab's edge, computing positions and scales so each one sits properly on the floor with its bottom just above the ground, and planning to add moss tufts and scattered plant elements across the base slab and pebbles.

For flowers, I'm picking manual ledge positions on the base slab top and writing a helper that raycasts downward onto the slab surface to get the correct landing height for each one.

For mushrooms, I'm designing the shape as a lathe profile: a separate stem rod and a rounded cap outline defined by a series of radius/height points to get a bulging mushroom cap silhouette.

For details, I'm scattering a few cream-colored sphere dots across the upper cap surface to mimic spots, and setting up a mush(x,z,scale) helper that positions the stem and cap on top of a surface hit. I also need to add whiskers as small rods extending outward from the muzzle sides at a few different angles.

Beyond the eye decal, I'm thinking through facial markings like a white eyebrow patch and dark eye rings typical of a red panda, plus a small tapered tuft on the forehead, and I may add a couple tiny cream fang cones peeking from the mouth corners for a cute touch.

I'm deciding whether to build the jaw as a separate, posable piece so the mouth can open slightly — maybe 5-6 degrees — to show a hint of teeth and a small pink tongue, giving it a cute half-smile rather than keeping the mouth fully closed.

Next I'm sketching the glowing dendro elements: a scattering of small glowing octahedra motes near the stone and several flat leaf-shaped glow petals that float and rotate around the creature for a bioluminescent effect.

After checking the part count stays under budget, I'm starting to write out the actual TypeScript file, defining head coat coordinates and a procedural paint function that shapes the eye patch and coat pattern based on normalized position on the head.

Still refining color zones...

Bumping the patch radius to 0.4 should work fine. For the eye decal, I'm calculating the hit point position based on azimuth and elevation angles relative to the head sphere center, adjusting the eye's vertical offset to about 0.03 in normalized coordinates.

Checking x placement for azimuth 32° — sin32 gives roughly 0.53, consistent with ellipsoid ray projection. I'm defining the tear streak as a darker brown region below the eye bottom, bounded by y-range and horizontal distance from center. For the eyebrow, I'm checking its normalized position doesn't collide with the ear root, placing it just below the ear base. The nose will be a flat dark ink color, and I'm skipping a separate nose bridge stripe for now, moving on to the cel-shaded outline style.

Working through leg paint using fur-edge coloring with tooth/period parameters for a jagged coat texture, then setting up decal placement on the skull surface and the body sweep geometry with a faceted sides count. I'm iterating over cheek spike positions at various azimuth/elevation angles and lengths, casting hits against the skull surface to place small cream-colored spikes with outward-and-back orientation.

Now I'm setting up the ear geometry via an extrude operation, mirroring it symmetrically for both sides using sign-based axis flips, and verifying the cross product math to confirm the front face normal points correctly outward for each ear.

I'm starting to write the actual build function, defining the skeleton joints (base, hips) with positions for the red panda model.

Now I'm setting up the spine chain and beginning a loop to construct the legs symmetrically for both left and right sides, defining shoulder and wrist positions for the front limbs...

Still writing skeleton joints...

Still figuring out joint parenting...

Attaching the paw to the tip joint with a dark flat cel color. I'm reconsidering toe geometry—rather than 64 separate toe and claw parts across all paws, I should merge the toe spheres per paw into single geometries to stay efficient.

Writing paw helper function...

Positioning claws...

Checking that part coloring just reuses existing geometry UVs, and confirming the body sweep follows the spine chain with the hip joint as the starting bone so the rear cap attaches to spine1 correctly.

Now I'm setting up the tail chain parented to hips with its own tapered sweep radius and ring coloring. For the neck, I'm picking a rust/coat tone slightly narrower than the head radius so it reads as tapering into the skull, then noting I'll skip chest bib patches for now and move on to scattering surface detail cards on the body before starting the collar band.

I'm computing a ring of 14 points around the midpoint of the neck chain, sizing it slightly larger than the neck ellipse so it sits just outside the surface, and confirming it clears the chest cap sphere so the band doesn't get swallowed. The ring tilts to match the neck's forward-and-up tangent direction, and I'm about to loft a teal-colored tube through the ring's points using a closed Catmull-Rom path for the collar band itself.

Placing gold studs at each ring item, offset slightly outward along its local axis, sized small enough to embed into the sweep radius...

Now I'm working out where the pendant should sit on the neck—trying to locate the front-facing point by angle or raycasting against the neck sweep, since the head occludes a direct hit test, so I'll just estimate coordinates directly instead.

I'm working through the geometry of the ring's tilted plane, computing the perpendicular directions to find where the front point of the collar/pendant actually sits relative to the chest surface, trying to pin down coordinates that don't exceed the chest boundary.

Letting the pendant hang slightly away from the chest with a short chain feels physically fine since gravity pulls it forward off the body. I'll compute the lowest point of the collar band by finding the band item with minimum y, then position the pendant ring just below that point.

Below the ring I'll add a glowing octahedron gem with a slightly larger gold frame behind it, plus five tassel strands hanging from the gem's bottom. This all seems plausible, so I'll move on to drafting the full file, estimating around 600 lines, starting with texture definitions like a tuft shape built from an SVG path.

Writing moss texture SVG...

Now I'm sketching the flower sprite: a green stem with five pale pink-lavender petals around a yellow center, plus a couple of leaves. Then moving on to the fern design, planning a central rib with leaflets branching off it.

Designing the rune glow next: a ring with an inner leaf-shaped glyph and small decorative ticks and dots, scaling the strokes to fit a larger raster size. Then I sketch a gold plaque with a rounded rectangular border, inner trim line, curled corner details, and small diamond accents at the edges, keeping the interior transparent.

Now for the tassel, I'm drawing it hanging downward with a gold cap band at the root and fanning strands below in two gold tones, matching how it attaches at the root edge. I'm skipping toe pad details and instead verifying that the scatter/frame hit functions correctly position flowers and hanging moss at their surface hit points.

For moss cards, coloring only matters for non-colored SVGs, so flowers won't need a tint pass. I'm setting up the scatter call on the main slab top with a random seed, minimum distance, and a filter requiring high moss mask values and upward-facing normals, sizing the clumps around 0.056 by 0.035 with some variation and spin for natural randomness, using cross-planes so they're visible from any angle — tallying roughly 90 tufts on the main slab, 90 on the base, and 20 on the pebbles.

Now I'm working out the hanging rim moss: scattering on the main slab but filtering for points near the rim edges, sized smaller at [0.035, 0.045], with around 40 cards. The tricky part is orienting these correctly so they hang from the top edge against the wall rather than poking through the slab interior — I'm deciding to use wall-normal hits instead, filtering for near-vertical normals and upper wall positions where the moss mask is already strong, so the card planes align with the wall surface and face outward along the wall's own normal direction.
